checks.location: Appendix C.3 after Eq (26); Algorithm 1 steps 16-18
checks.claim: Replacing the model expectation by a single offline next-state sample yields an objective optimisable by standard SGD.
checks.explanation: A single next-state plug-in is biased inside the nonlinear dual term.
checks.demonstration: An unbiased sample inside a convex nonlinear function does not give an unbiased function estimate. For \(\phi_+^*(y)=\tfrac12[y+1]_+^2-\tfrac12\), equal next values \(\pm0.5\), and \(\beta=1\), the sample-function expectation is \(0.125\), while the function of the mean is zero. The text acknowledges a single-sample plug-in, which is a different surrogate.

checks.scope: The sample surrogate differs from the dual objective; the duality result itself is not disproved.
checks.claimContext: The dual uses \(\phi_+^*\) of a residual containing \(\mathbb E_P[\nu_{t+1}]\). Algorithm 1 instead feeds one sampled next-state value through that nonlinear function.
checks.title: A single next-state plug-in is biased inside the nonlinear dual term

checks.location: Algorithm 1 step 18 versus Eq (10)/Eq (26)
checks.claim: The step-18 empirical loss is the sample form of the finite-horizon dual Eq (26).
checks.explanation: A flat transition mean rescales only one part of the finite-horizon dual.
checks.demonstration: A uniformly pooled mean estimates \(H^{-1}\sum_t\mathbb E_{d_t^D}[\cdot]\). The other two terms are not divided by \(H\), so this is not a harmless overall loss scaling. Multiplying the full flat loss by \(H\) instead overweights those other terms and can change the optimizer.
checks.repair: Multiply the pooled flow mean by \(H\), use appropriately weighted per-time sampling, or explicitly define an unnormalized transition measure consistent with the dual.
checks.scope: The empirical loss needs a measure/normalization convention; the finite-horizon dual remains a separate valid expression.
checks.claimContext: The dual sums flow terms over \(H\) time steps, alongside initial-state and conjugate terms. Algorithm 1 uses a flat mean over the pooled transition dataset without horizon weighting.
checks.title: A flat transition mean rescales only one part of the finite-horizon dual

review-neurips-2026-151918.title: NormLift: From Lifted Features To Semantic Reliability In 3D Gaussian Splatting

checks.location: Appendix E.2, paragraph after rank correlations
checks.claim: The independence baseline for Jaccard overlap of two lowest-20% sets is .20, making observed .162 below independent overlap.
checks.explanation: The value \(0.20\) is the conditional fraction of one independent set lying in the other, not their population Jaccard ratio. The stated baseline uses the wrong denominator and reverses the comparison with the population independence benchmark.
checks.demonstration:
For independent selection indicators \(A,B\), each with probability \(p=0.2\),
\[\Pr(A\cap B)=p^2=0.04,\qquad\Pr(A\cup B)=2p-p^2=0.36.\]
The population Jaccard ratio is therefore
\[J_{\mathrm{ind}}=\frac{p^2}{2p-p^2}=\frac19\approx0.1111.\]
The reported \(0.162\) is above this benchmark. For two uniformly random fixed-size sets of size \(m=N/5\), the finite-sample null instead has \(I\sim\operatorname{Hypergeom}(N,m,m)\) and expectation \(\mathbb E[I/(2m-I)]\); it converges to \(1/9\) and should not be confused with the ratio of expectations. The source supplies neither this finite-population calculation nor a reason to use the conditional-overlap value \(0.20\).
checks.repair: Replace the population independence baseline by \(1/9\) and state that \(0.162\) is above it. If a finite-sample test is intended, use the actual population and set sizes with the hypergeometric overlap distribution, computing \(\mathbb E[I/(2m-I)]\) or a tail probability. Retain the observed Jaccard value and the separately reported rank correlations; those quantities do not change under this correction.
checks.scope: Unchanged auxiliary probability calculation in v2. The finding concerns the mathematical null baseline and its comparison, not segmentation rankings, timings or a claim that the measured overlap was computed incorrectly. No statistical significance is inferred from the aggregate value alone.
checks.title: The independent-set Jaccard baseline is about 0.111, not 0.20
checks.claimContext: Appendix E.2 of v2 compares two sets containing the lowest \(20\%\) of Gaussians by reliability and opacity. It calls their Jaccard overlap \(0.162\) below an independence baseline of \(0.20\). Jaccard overlap is intersection size divided by union size.
checks.whyItMatters: The independence comparison changes direction, while the underlying observations and method remain outside this mathematical correction.
checks.verificationNote: Compared retained source text with arXiv:2609.18898v2 (2026-10-21). The relevant assertion and hypotheses are unchanged; checkedLocation identifies current numbering. The derived grade is narrowed to the actual current mathematical scope; the historical verdict and severity are preserved.
checks.checkedLocation: v2 Appendix E.2, paragraph following the Spearman and Kendall correlations for positive-reliability Gaussians.

review-neurips-2026-151918.issueTitle: The Jaccard independence comparison uses the wrong denominator
review-neurips-2026-151918.plainExplanation: For two independent \(20\%\) selections, the population Jaccard baseline is \(1/9\), approximately \(0.111\), so \(0.162\) is above that benchmark. This corrects an auxiliary probability comparison; it does not alter the measured overlap or the separately reported rank correlations.
